target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- Internal delivery paths become code-aware without changing the public contract: the low-level `packages/tool-call-repair` stripper takes an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline, `sanitizeUserFacingText`, and the visible-text sanitizer, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed on those internal paths.
- The exported plugin SDK helper `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it scrubs tool-call-shaped blocks even inside code regions, matching current main), preserving the upgrade contract for third-party callers that use it to sanitize untrusted visible text. Code-aware behavior is available as an explicit opt-in via `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }`; the default remains a strict scrubber.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer); the exported SDK helper's default behavior is unchanged from main (strict), with code-awareness added only as an opt-in and to internal delivery call sites; and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

Exported SDK helper contract (strict default): the `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` tests lock both modes — with no options the helper strips a tool-call-shaped block even when it sits inside a Markdown code fence or inline span (strict scrubber, matching main), while `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` preserves the same fenced/inline example verbatim. Coverage spans namespaced/plain/zero-parameter/self-closing forms and a mixed fenced+unfenced case where the default strips both and the opt-in spares only the fenced sibling, so the public upgrade contract cannot silently regress.

Local validation:

```
vitest src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts: 50 pass (incl. dual-mode strict-default + preserveCodeRegions opt-in locks)
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
vitest src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts + src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.test.ts: pass
node scripts/check-plugin-sdk-subpath-exports.mjs: OK
pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check: OK (baseline regenerated for the additive signature change)
pnpm tsgo:core: clean
git diff --check: clean
```





---

## Follow-up fix: mixed prose + parametrized invoke on the persist path

The initial scope covered zero-argument / self-closing invoke blocks. A separate, related leak was found afterward from a real captured session: a model turn that emits **leading visible prose** followed by a **fully-closed, parametrized** `invoke` block (namespaced or bare).

Root cause: `scrubOverCapPlainTextToolCallMessage` classifies such a turn as buffer state `"impossible"` (the leading prose means it is not a buffered tool-call prefix). When under the buffer cap it returned `undefined`, so the raw message was persisted and leaked to chat. The display path (`sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` → line-scanning `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) already strips this block, but the persist/normalize path did not, so the two diverged. Promotion cannot run for these blocks because a non-zero-offset block never parses as standalone.

Fix: before the `impossible` + under-cap `return undefined`, apply the same line-standalone `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` to each text block of the message content and return the scrubbed message, giving persist ↔ display parity. Behavior is byte-identical when nothing strips; tool execution is not widened (no auto-promotion).

Added mixed-content regression tests (bare and namespaced) asserting the persisted message carries no raw invoke XML, preserves prose up to the boundary, and does not auto-promote.

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

### Performance impact

- Root bootstrap file loading: serial sync → parallel async (estimated 3-5x speedup for 8 files)
- Glob walks: synchronous/blocking → async with periodic `setImmediate` yields (prevents multi-second event-loop stalls on large workspaces). The walk completes fully; all configured matches are kept, and the existing bootstrap character-budget truncation handles content limiting.
- Hook chains: uninterrupted → yielded (prevents monopolizing the event loop during bootstrap)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, which blocks the loop and drops messages. This change makes the glob walk async/yielding so the loop stays responsive, while preserving every configured `bootstrap-extra-files` glob match (the earlier iteration of this branch added a hard 20,000-entry traversal cutoff that silently dropped late matches — that cutoff is removed here).
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFiles` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. Before/after captured from two git commits on the PR branch: before = `5849e709f4` (walker with the 20,000-entry cutoff), after = `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed).
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of ~26,100 filesystem entries (a 3-tier tree, 30×30×28 filler files) with a single configured-glob target `AGENTS.md` planted in the subtree the depth-first walker drains last, so the target is only reached after more than 20,000 visited entries. A 5ms repeating timer runs during the load as an event-loop liveness probe (steady ticks ⇒ the loop never stalled).
- **Failing proof before fix**: commit `5849e709f4` (cutoff present):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 82.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 16 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 0
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: false
  RESULT: late configured glob match was DROPPED (pre-fix behavior)
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```
  # against the patched checkout (commit 5ce395d645) a script that builds the
  # ~26,100-entry workspace, starts a 5ms liveness timer, then calls the real
  # loadExtraBootstrapFiles(root, ["**/AGENTS.md"]) and checks the deep match:
  npx tsx proof-live.mts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**: terminal output from `node`/`tsx` against commit `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 99.4ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 20 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 1
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: true
  RESULT: configured glob match beyond old cutoff is PRESERVED; event loop stayed live
  ```
- **Observed result after fix**: With the cutoff removed, the configured `**/AGENTS.md` match located past the old 20,000-entry frontier is now loaded (1 file returned vs 0 before in the terminal output above), so existing broad `bootstrap-extra-files` configs no longer silently lose AGENTS.md/TOOLS.md context. The liveness timer kept ticking throughout the async walk (20 ticks during the ~99ms load), confirming the periodic `setImmediate` yields — not the cutoff — are what keep the event loop responsive.
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real glob-resolution code path and event-loop liveness directly rather than through a connected channel. The focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

Closes #87509

target.title: Dashboard: stream + computed data-binding kinds
target.body:
> 📦 **Part of the modular-dashboard package** — master hub **#101136** (architecture diagrams · bottom-up merge order · the full per-PR test map).
>
> 🧪 **Try this PR:** bind a widget with `stream:` or `computed:` → the stream comes from the allowlisted gateway events; `computed` is a fixed op set with **no eval**.

---


> Live push feeds and derived values, not just files: bind a widget to a gateway event stream, or compute one from other bindings — safely, with no new network and no expression language.

Closes #101150. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review the `schema.ts` / `index.ts` / `data-read.ts` deltas.

## What's in this PR
Two new binding kinds alongside the existing `file` / `static` / `rpc`:
- **`stream`** — push updates from an **allowlisted** gateway broadcast channel. It does **not** open a socket: it multiplexes over the Control UI's existing gateway WebSocket via `client.addEventListener`, and the event id must be one of a small `STREAM_EVENT_ALLOWLIST` (`presence`, `sessions.changed`, `plugin.dashboard.changed` — all read-only). Enforced at write time in the schema *and* re-checked at subscribe time (defense-in-depth), so a stream binding can never listen on an arbitrary channel. Unsubscribes on unmount.
- **`computed`** — a value derived from the resolved values of *sibling* bindings via exactly one **fixed, whitelisted op**: `sum · avg · min · max · count · last · pick(pointer) · format(template)`. It's a `switch` — **no expression language, no `eval`, no `Function`**. `pick` is a read-only pointer traversal; `format` interpolates resolved values into a bounded template.

**Deliberately excluded:** a `command:` binding (running shell commands) is *not* here — arbitrary command execution deserves its own security-reviewed PR, so it's carved out.

## How it works & why it's safe
`resolveBinding` gains branches on both sides (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/index.ts` client, `extensions/dashboard/src/data-read.ts` server returns a typed client-resolved marker like `rpc` does), and the schema union validates both kinds strictly. Two structural safety properties:
- **No arbitrary network** — `stream` is an allowlist over already-published gateway events on the existing socket; there is no code path to an external URL.
- **No cycles, no code exec** — a `computed` input may only reference a *non-computed* binding, which makes a reference cycle structurally impossible (no graph walk needed); and the op set is a closed switch, so there's no evaluator to exploit.

No new dependency.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Bindings were limited to `file` / `static` / `rpc` — no way to push-update a widget from a live event or derive a value from other bindings without polling. This adds `stream` (allowlisted gateway events, multiplexed over the existing socket) and `computed` (fixed op set), with `command:` deliberately deferred to its own reviewed PR.
**Evidence:** `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/dashboard` + `pnpm -C ui vitest run src/lib/dashboard` green — schema accept/reject for both kinds (unknown op, malformed inputs, non-allowlisted event, computed→computed rejection), each computed op's result, and stream subscribe→push→unsubscribe over a mocked event source; `pnpm ui:i18n:check`, `pnpm ui:build`, full type-aware oxlint clean. Counts confirmed by the submitting orchestrator's own gate run.

target.body:
> 📦 **Part of the modular-dashboard package** — master hub **#101136** (architecture diagrams · bottom-up merge order · the full per-PR test map).
>
> 🧪 **Try it:** this is the foundation (backend control plane). Check out the top of the foundation stack — **#101098** — to run the whole feature in one branch; then follow the hub's per-PR test map.

---

# dashboard plugin: workspace document + control plane (1/3)

> **The dashboard your agent builds with you.** This PR is the foundation: one guarded document, one store, three faces (gateway RPC, CLI, agent tools) that all funnel through it. No UI yet — that's PR2. This is the plumbing that makes "agent and human edit the same layout" possible at all.

This PR has no UI, but its whole point is what happens on the wire. Here the control plane is doing exactly what it exists to do: an agent's `dashboard.tab.create` / `dashboard.widget.add` calls land in the store and compose a live tab (the overlay chips are the real RPCs firing) — the same validated path a human's CLI call takes.

![An agent composing a Financials tab through the dashboard.* control plane — overlay chips show the real dashboard.tab.create / dashboard.widget.add RPCs firing against the store](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/02-financials-tab-appears-live.png)

> **Stack note.** This is the base of a three-PR stack (#101094 here → #101097 UI → #101098 custom widgets); each later PR targets `main` and builds cumulatively on this one. This PR is self-contained — `extensions/dashboard` only, zero core changes — and independently mergeable/useful on its own.

## What problem this solves

Right now there's no shared, structured place for "what does this operator's dashboard look like" to live — any composability has to be hand-coded per view. Two audiences need this: operators who want to lay out their own control hub without touching code, and agents that want to build that layout *for* them. Both need the same underlying guarantee — one validated document, no partial writes, no path where a human's layout and an agent's layout can silently diverge.

## What's in this PR

- `extensions/dashboard` — a new bundled plugin, `enabledByDefault: true`, zero core-file changes (`git diff --stat` is scoped entirely to the plugin directory).
- **`workspace.json`** — the layout-as-data document (tabs → widgets → grid position → data bindings), owned at `<stateDir>/dashboard/workspace.json`, `schemaVersion`-migrated on read.
- **`DashboardStore`** — the single writer. Atomic writes (`replaceFileAtomic`), async-mutex-serialized mutations, a 256 KB size cap, a 32-tab / 24-widget-per-tab cap, and a 20-entry undo ring. Every mutation is validated by hand-written guards (repo idiom — no schema library at the RPC layer); invalid ops are rejected whole, never partially applied.
- **14 gateway methods** (`dashboard.*`) covering tab CRUD/reorder, widget CRUD/move/batch-layout, widget approval, full-document replace (bulk agent authoring), undo, and a scoped data-read endpoint — each correctly scoped `operator.read` or `operator.write`.
- **Change broadcasts** — every successful write fires `plugin.dashboard.changed { workspaceVersion, changedTabSlug, actor }` so every connected operator UI can live-update. Reads never broadcast; failed writes never broadcast.
- **Data bindings, not fetches** — widgets declare a `file` (path-jailed under `<stateDir>/dashboard/data/`) or `static` binding; nothing in this layer lets a widget make an arbitrary network call. (An `rpc` binding kind exists in the schema for write-time validation, but is resolved client-side by the trusted Control UI in PR2/PR3 — this plugin's gateway handlers cannot dispatch other gateway methods at this HEAD, so `dashboard.data.read` intentionally does not proxy `rpc` bindings. Noted here because it shaped the schema.)
- **CLI + agent tools** (this PR includes both, since they're thin callers over the same store): `openclaw dashboard tabs/widgets/layout …` from a terminal, and 14 `dashboard_*` agent tools with typebox schemas — both call the identical in-process validated path the gateway RPC uses. Agent-originated writes are stamped `createdBy: "agent:<id>"` from tool context; this is never overridable via tool params.

## See it

The image above is this control plane in action. The whole end-to-end series — CLI call, agent tool call, and the UI layers on top — is in the animated demo on the tracking issue and the integration PR.

## How it works

The design goal is a single contract: **one validated document, one writer, three faces.** Humans and agents both compose the operator's dashboard, and they must never be able to diverge — so every mutation, no matter who originates it, goes through the exact same code path.

### `workspace.json` — layout as data

The dashboard's entire state is one JSON document at `<stateDir>/dashboard/workspace.json` (state dir via `resolveStateDir()`, default `~/.openclaw`). It is *layout-as-data*: tabs contain widgets, widgets carry a grid position, data bindings, and provenance. Nothing about a workspace lives in code — it's all this document.

```jsonc
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "workspaceVersion": 42,               // monotonic; bumped on every accepted write
  "tabs": [
    {
      "slug": "financials",             // ^[a-z0-9-]{1,40}$ — also the deep-link key
      "title": "Financials",
      "icon": "barChart",
      "hidden": false,
      "createdBy": "agent:main",        // provenance: "user" | "system" | "agent:<id>"
      "widgets": [
        {
          "id": "w_rev_q3",
          "kind": "builtin:stat-card",  // "builtin:<name>" | "custom:<name>"
          "title": "Q3 Revenue",
          "grid": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 4, "h": 2 },   // 12-column grid units
          "collapsed": false,
          "bindings": {
            "value": { "source": "file", "path": "q3.json", "pointer": "/revenue" }
          },
          "props": { "format": "usd" }
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "widgetsRegistry": {                  // custom-widget install/approval state (PR3)
    "revenue-chart": { "status": "approved", "approvedBy": "user", "createdBy": "agent:main" }
  },
  "prefs": { "tabOrder": ["main", "financials"] }
}
```

`schemaVersion` is migrated on read; future versions are rejected rather than guessed at.

### `DashboardStore` — the sole writer

`DashboardStore` is the only thing in the codebase that writes this file. Its `mutate(fn, { actor })` path is deliberately boring and total:

1. acquire a single in-process **async mutex** (serializes every caller in the one gateway process — RPC, CLI, and agent tools alike);
2. `structuredClone` the current doc and apply `fn` to the *draft*;
3. run `validateWorkspaceDoc(draft)` — hand-written guards, no schema library at the RPC layer (repo idiom);
4. enforce the caps (≤ 256 KB serialized, ≤ 32 tabs, ≤ 24 widgets/tab);
5. push the previous serialization onto a **20-entry undo ring** under `<stateDir>/dashboard/undo/`;
6. `replaceFileAtomic` (temp file + rename) and bump `workspaceVersion`.

Any validation failure throws before step 5 — **rejects are whole; nothing is ever partially applied**, and the file on disk is never touched by a rejected write. Because a single process owns the file and the mutex serializes callers, there is no interleaving and no last-writer-wins race.

### 14 `dashboard.*` methods, correctly scoped

The store is fronted by 14 gateway methods, each registered with an explicit scope — reads are `operator.read`, writes are `operator.write`:

| Reads (`operator.read`) | Writes (`operator.write`) |
|---|---|
| `dashboard.workspace.get` | `dashboard.tab.create` · `dashboard.tab.update` · `dashboard.tab.delete` · `dashboard.tab.reorder` |
| `dashboard.data.read` | `dashboard.widget.add` · `dashboard.widget.update` · `dashboard.widget.move` · `dashboard.widget.remove` · `dashboard.widget.setLayout` |
| | `dashboard.widget.approve` · `dashboard.workspace.replace` (bulk agent authoring) · `dashboard.workspace.undo` |

Validation is hand-written param readers per method (throwing typed errors), copied from the `extensions/workboard` idiom rather than a zod layer — so review reads the same as the rest of the repo.

### One store, three faces — the same validated path

This is the crux. The CLI and the agent tools are *thin callers over the same store instance*, not parallel implementations:

- **Gateway RPC** `dashboard.*` — used by the Control UI (PR2) and the CLI.
- **CLI** `openclaw dashboard tabs/widgets/layout …` — a plugin-registered CLI that calls the RPC.
- **Agent tools** `dashboard_*` (14 tools, typebox input schemas) — call the store **in-process**, hitting the identical validation + broadcast.

```
  openclaw dashboard tabs create --title Financials   (CLI, actor defaults to "user")
                            │
  dashboard_tab_create  ────┤   (agent tool, actor stamped "agent:<id>" from tool context)
                            │
  dashboard.tab.create  ────┤   (gateway RPC from the Control UI)
                            ▼
                     DashboardStore.mutate()   ← one mutex, one validator, one atomic write
                            ▼
                     workspace.json  +  plugin.dashboard.changed broadcast
```

A human's `openclaw dashboard tabs create --title Financials` and an agent's `dashboard_tab_create` tool call produce byte-identical documents through byte-identical validation — the only difference is the `createdBy` stamp, which is set from the caller's context (`agent:<id>` for tools) and **can never be overridden via tool params**. That is what makes "agent and human edit the same layout" a guarantee rather than a hope.

### Change broadcasts

Every *successful write* ends with `opts.context.broadcast("plugin.dashboard.changed", { workspaceVersion, changedTabSlug, actor })`, so every connected operator UI can live-update (PR2 subscribes to this). Reads never broadcast; failed writes never broadcast. The payload is intentionally minimal — receivers refetch; the whole document is never shipped in an event.

### Bindings, not fetches

Widgets *declare* data sources; this layer never lets a widget make an arbitrary call. A binding is a `file` (path-jailed under `<stateDir>/dashboard/data/`, reusing the canvas logical-path-normalization idiom) or a `static` literal, resolved by `dashboard.data.read`. An `rpc` binding kind also exists in the schema and is validated at write time against `DATA_READ_RPC_ALLOWLIST` — but it is deliberately **not** proxied by this plugin's handlers: at this HEAD, plugin gateway-method handlers cannot dispatch other gateway methods (SDK gate `gatewayMethodDispatchAllowed`), so `rpc` bindings are resolved client-side by the trusted Control UI over its own authenticated socket (same authz boundary). `dashboard.data.read` returns a typed `binding_client_resolved` for them. This is noted here because it shaped the schema, and PR2/PR3 depend on it.

Everything above is `extensions/dashboard` only — `git diff --stat` is scoped entirely to the plugin directory. **Zero core-file changes.**

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** There is no shared, validated document for an operator's dashboard layout, so any composability has to be hand-coded per view and a human's layout and an agent's layout can silently diverge. This PR adds `extensions/dashboard` — one `workspace.json` document and one `DashboardStore` fronted by 14 gateway methods, a CLI, and 14 agent tools, so every write (RPC, CLI, or agent tool) funnels through one validated, atomic, undoable path.

**Evidence:** The `extensions/dashboard` test suite passes via `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/dashboard` — store atomicity, the 20-entry undo ring (21st mutation evicts oldest; undo restores exactly), size/count caps, every schema reject path (slug charset, dup slugs, grid overflow, kind pattern, binding union, `createdBy` pattern), gateway-method registration/scoping, the binding resolver, and a concurrency test proving two mutations serialize under the mutex; `tsgo` and oxlint clean. The control plane in action — an agent's `dashboard.tab.create` / `dashboard.widget.add` RPCs composing a live tab through the store — is the screenshot above and the end-to-end recording on the tracking issue.

## Verification

**Size:** ~3,300 lines of source across 11 files (the backend + control plane, excluding tests) — well inside VISION.md's ~5K reviewable-line guideline. The full PR is 19 files including its test suite.

- Full unit suite for the store, schema validation (every reject path — slug charset, duplicate slugs, grid overflow, kind pattern, binding union, size/count caps, `createdBy` pattern — has a dedicated test), gateway method registration/scoping, and the binding resolver.
- Concurrency test: two concurrent mutations serialize correctly under the mutex.
- Undo-ring test: the 21st mutation evicts the oldest snapshot; undo restores exactly the prior document.
- The `extensions/dashboard` test suite (store, schema, gateway methods, CLI, agent tools, binding resolver) and `tsgo`/oxlint pass. CI runs on this PR.

## Closes / part of

Part of #101093. Foundation for #101097, #101098 — neither later PR is reachable without this one merged first.

target.title: fix: fail release performance when reports do not publish
target.body:
Closes #103125

_AI-assisted maintainer release fix._

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where release maintainers could receive a green performance workflow even though the required Clawgrit baseline report was never published. In [run 29051458125](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29051458125), the release-profile Kova evaluation passed, but report authentication failed on all five push attempts and the workflow still exited successfully with only an optional-publish warning.

## Why This Change Was Made

The workflow now resolves the tested SHA once, keeps publisher credentials out of every target-code/Kova runner, and publishes only from a fresh Ubuntu job consuming validated workflow artifacts. Only after artifact validation and report-commit preparation does it mint a short-lived ClawSweeper GitHub App token scoped to `openclaw/clawgrit-reports` contents-write; the token is passed only to a command-scoped Git push header and is revoked by the pinned token action's default post-step. The publisher uses a plain remote, disables Git hooks, rejects non-canonical/symlink/special-file inputs, and replays concurrent report commits against the current reports tip while retaining a unique run path and a deterministic latest pointer.

Publication is fail-closed for scheduled and `profile=release` runs, including full release validation. Manually dispatched non-release diagnostics remain advisory by design because their uploaded workflow artifacts are useful even when they are not authoritative release evidence.

The Kova evaluator is pinned to `36dda3731db1e62fc4a1c47c43257c15cb173c7f`. [Kova #11](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/11) makes a successful HTTP health response prove TCP readiness even when the gateway begins listening between sequential probes; [Kova #12](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/12) hardens that regression selfcheck against port reuse; [Kova #13](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/13) readiness-gates bundled-plugin startup before automatic auth config mutation; and [Kova #16](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/16) pins the evidence-calibrated bundled-plugin gateway contract at 950 MiB RSS / 250% CPU with raw and resolved-policy selfchecks.

## User Impact

Release operators can trust a green scheduled/full performance gate to mean both evaluation and durable report publication succeeded. Diagnostic users keep artifact access without an unrelated reports-repository outage turning every manual non-release experiment red. There is no end-user runtime behavior change.

## Evidence

- Reproduction: [run 29051458125](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29051458125/job/86232944434) shows five `Invalid username or token` push failures followed by a successful job conclusion.
- Exact-branch release proof: [run 29054521133](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29054521133) minted the scoped App token and all three publisher jobs succeeded. `clawgrit-reports` advanced from `461b70022600` to [`dae06ab6725d`](https://github.com/openclaw/clawgrit-reports/commit/dae06ab6725dbb61c5298a815ee691e1af3c9a6f); the durable pointer records workflow/tested SHA `c7e1f275ccd3`, run `29054521133-1`, and the unique `mock-provider` report path. The overall run exposed a separate Kova readiness-probe race and correctly remained red; its durable failure report proves publication is independent of evaluator success.
- Kova robustness fixes: [Kova #11](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/11) covers the observed same-iteration TCP-failure/health-success race; [Kova #12](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/12) removes a selfcheck port-reuse race; [Kova #13](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/13) fixes a real bundled-plugin startup/config-migration ordering race found by repeat proof; and [Kova #16](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/pull/16) preserves explicit 950 MiB RSS / 250% CPU workload limits with raw/resolved selfchecks after full readiness made the real 812–870 MiB envelope visible. Their Node 24 Linux/macOS CI runs [29055328087](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/actions/runs/29055328087), [29055520988](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/actions/runs/29055520988), [29056313238](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/actions/runs/29056313238), and [29057891921](https://github.com/openclaw/Kova/actions/runs/29057891921) are green; OpenClaw pins merged head `36dda3731db1`.
- Exact f506 release proof: [run 29055648771](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29055648771) passed 18/18 at Kova `188458041821`; all publisher jobs succeeded and `clawgrit-reports` advanced to [`00737c600fc6`](https://github.com/openclaw/clawgrit-reports/commit/00737c600fc6d5cbceeb6bc40e546f66b19155fc) with the exact latest pointer.
- Final Blacksmith Testbox proof on commit `c7e1f275ccd3` (lease `tbx_01kx4ewhnz6gkdjnmrty34x32r`, [carrier run 29053719092](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29053719092)): wrapper exit 0; focused workflow suite 21/21; `pnpm check:workflows`/zizmor passed; full docs checks passed with 0 broken links.
- The focused suite covers exact GitHub App client/repository/permission scope, one private-key reference, one token consumer, token creation only after artifact validation, required/advisory policy, missing-token/no-push behavior, artifact-attempt reuse, unsafe-path rejection, successful/failed push summaries, and concurrent bare-repository writers preserving both reports.
- Broad source-commit validation: `pnpm check:changed`, `pnpm check:workflows`/zizmor, full docs checks, actionlint, targeted oxfmt, docs formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh clean cherry-pick onto `b8537cd81ef59bfbe63580b8fb08adbb876ea5b0`: no conflicts; `actionlint .github/workflows/openclaw-performance.yml` and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passed.
- Independent credential-boundary review and final GPT-5.5/high autoreview: no findings; patch correct at 0.82 confidence.

target.body:
> 📦 **Part of the modular-dashboard package** — master hub **#101136** (architecture diagrams · bottom-up merge order · the full per-PR test map).
>
> 🧪 **Try this PR:** add a `builtin:preview` widget bound to a URL and reload → the live embed renders in the sandbox; the reload/verify controls work.

---

> A live preview panel in the dashboard: embed a running dev server or a deployed URL, with reload and device-frame controls.

Closes #101138 (phase 1). **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review the new `preview` widget files as the delta.

## What problem this solves
Operators and maintainers have asked for a browser/preview panel in the dashboard for a long time (#27574). This delivers phase 1: a trusted `builtin:preview` widget that renders a URL inside the same sandboxed embed frame the dashboard already uses, with reload + viewport controls — so a preview is just another widget an agent or human can place.

## What's in this PR
- A new `builtin:preview` widget (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/widgets/preview.ts`) cloned from `iframe-embed`, reusing its sandbox + external-URL policy unchanged.
- Chrome: a reload control, and desktop / tablet / mobile viewport presets that constrain the frame width (default via a widget prop).
- Registered in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS`; `preview` added to `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN`.
- Unit tests: renders the bound URL sandboxed, reload re-sets the frame src, the viewport switch resizes the frame, and the sandbox + external-URL policy match iframe-embed. The UI dashboard suite (100 tests) is green.

## Scope
Phase 1 only — embed + reload + viewport. Phase 2 (agent-driven dev-server lifecycle + hot-reload) and phase 3 (browser-backed console/network/screenshot so the agent sees its own preview) are follow-on PRs tracked on #101138.

## How it works
The preview widget reuses `resolveEmbedSandbox` and the external-URL gating from `iframe-embed` verbatim — it does **not** weaken the sandbox. The URL comes from the same `static`/`rpc` binding path every builtin uses. The added chrome (reload, viewport) is pure view state around the existing sandboxed frame.

Note: **no new dependency** — `pnpm-lock.yaml` is unchanged. The diff includes regenerated i18n locale bundles for the new `dashboard.widget.preview.*` keys (via the repo's `ui:i18n:sync` locale workflow); those generated files can be skipped in review.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** The dashboard has no preview/browser panel (#27574); there's no first-class way to watch a running dev server or a deployed URL inside a workspace. This adds a trusted `builtin:preview` widget with reload + viewport controls, reusing the existing sandboxed embed frame.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → 100 passed (the preview widget renders the bound URL in a sandboxed frame, the reload control re-sets `src`, viewport buttons swap the frame width, and the sandbox + external-URL policy match `iframe-embed`); `pnpm ui:build` green; oxlint clean; `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean after regenerating the locale bundles.

## What Problem This Solves

Static provider catalog conversion did not preserve all provider/model metadata consistently. The concrete current-main gap is provider-level `params`: static-catalog rows can define provider request params, but the returned runtime model did not merge those provider params with model params.

This PR also makes the static provider catalog converter explicitly carry `compat` and `mediaInput` so the returned runtime model preserves the same schema-valid metadata downstream payload and capability code expects.

## Why This Change Was Made

The runtime should preserve schema-valid provider/model metadata when resolving static provider catalog models. This is a metadata-propagation fix in `modelFromProviderStaticCatalog`; it does not add a new config key, policy path, transport, or custom-provider tool API.

Reviewer scope:
- This PR proves static provider catalog params/metadata propagation into the resolved runtime model and OpenAI-compatible request params via production modules.
- This PR is intentionally scoped away from the separate live-session `Tool exec not found` issue.
- Current main already keeps normal configured-provider compat flowing in other paths, and tools are permissive unless `compat.supportsTools === false`; the changed path here is static provider catalog conversion.

## User Impact

Users and bundled/provider catalogs can define provider-level request params and model metadata without losing that metadata during static provider catalog model resolution. Downstream payload generation and capability checks then receive the resolved model shape consistently.

Behavior or issue addressed:
- Static provider catalog conversion merges provider-level and model-level `params`, with model-level values taking precedence.
- Static provider catalog conversion preserves model `compat` metadata.
- Static provider catalog conversion preserves model `mediaInput` metadata.
- Real CLI proof exercises production modules `buildInlineProviderModels` + `buildOpenAICompletionsParams` + `supportsModelTools` and shows merged params reaching request payload.
- Regression coverage verifies that a resolved model with `compat.supportsTools=true` remains tool-capable through `supportsModelTools(model)`.

target.title: Interactive parity with the Codex runtime: ask-user-question · plan mode · goal mode
target.body:
> **The agent that asks, plans, and pursues.** This PR gives every OpenClaw session the three interactive primitives Codex-native users already have: the agent can ask structured questions (options + "(Recommended)" + free-text "Other", answerable from any surface), enter a real plan mode (read-only enforcement, a live plan panel, approve-to-execute), and pursue a long-running goal unattended behind a safety-gated continuation driver with a visible "Pursuing goal" chip.

Master hub: #102260 (architecture diagrams, the full test map, and the follow-up roadmap live there).

![Interactive parity demo: mode selector → plan mode with a live checklist in the right sidebar → inline approval → agent question answered inline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/c57fe74c64e15e1de7a76e742598904ff207c849/docs/assets/interactive-parity/parity-demo.gif)

*The full flow — plan mode, the live plan pane, inline approval, and an inline agent question. A [30s narrated walkthrough](https://github.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/releases/download/interactive-parity-media-v1/parity-demo.mp4) covers goal mode too.*

## Why this shape
The primitives were **already merged** (`update_plan` experimental, goal state tools, a codex user-input bridge, `stream:plan` events, exec-approval UI, Telegram/Slack buttons) — this PR is the completion layer, and every feature rides an existing choke point rather than inventing a parallel system. One branch, **take-apart commit groups** (reviewable and revertable independently; happy to split into stacked PRs on request) — the three feature groups, then a Control-UI pass bringing the surface to Codex-Desktop parity (inline composer cards, right-sidebar plan, mode selector, goal modal):

| Commits | Group | Delivers |
|---|---|---|
| 1–11 | **Question infra** | `ask_user_question` tool · global QuestionManager (exec-approval pattern) · `question.list/resolve` + events · Control-UI card · Telegram/Slack buttons + proactive push · `/answer` · restart expiry-sweep · codex-bridge convergence (structured vs free-text race) |
| 12–21 | **Plan mode** | plan-state slot + `enter/exit_plan_mode` · read-only gate at the single before-tool-call choke point · `update_plan` promoted default-on · live plan panel · `/plan` commands + structured channel summaries · exit-plan approval rides the question infra |
| 22–27 | **Goal mode** | continuation driver (debounced, 4-gated, never self-re-arms) · durable no-progress ceiling · `/goal set/edit/pause/resume/stop --budget` · "Pursuing goal" pill + edit modal · single-source `goal.updated` · behind `tools.experimental.goalDriver` |
| 28–36 | **Control-UI parity pass** | composer goal-pill Lit-race fix · questions & plan-approval as **inline composer cards** (modals retired) · active plan **docked in the right sidebar** · **mode selector** (off/plan/goal, mutually exclusive) by the gear · goal-editor **modal** with card chrome · whole-program type + lint clean |

## What each feature does

### 1 · Structured questions
`ask_user_question` (1-3 questions, 2-4 options, first recommended, auto-"Other") parks the *tool* on a global-manager promise — the exec-approval pattern — so the answer can come from anywhere: an **inline card in the chat composer** (Codex-Desktop style, not a page-locking modal), Telegram inline buttons or Slack Block Kit (pushed proactively to the turn-source chat, deduped), or `/answer <n|text>` on any channel. Ask on Telegram, answer in the browser. No default timeout (humans sleep); a gateway restart expires pending questions loudly (`question.expired`) instead of hanging. Codex-runtime sessions converge: their `request_user_input` (already held open as a JSON-RPC request) now renders the same card, racing the structured answer against the legacy next-free-text path.

![The agent's question rendered inline in the composer: numbered options, a Recommended chip, an "Other" free-text option, with 1-of-N paging](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/c57fe74c64e15e1de7a76e742598904ff207c849/docs/assets/interactive-parity/question-inline.png)

### 2 · Plan mode
The **mode selector by the gear** (or `/plan` / `enter_plan_mode`) puts the session in a read-only collaboration mode enforced as a **core policy at the one choke point every tool execution funnels through** — built-ins incl. exec and subagent spawn, plugin/MCP-backed, catalog, code-mode, client tools. The agent researches and maintains a live checklist (`update_plan`, promoted from experimental with a kill-switch) that ticks in real time in the **right-sidebar plan pane** (always viewable, full rendered plan; a compact chip stays inline); `exit_plan_mode` persists the plan to `~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/plans/` and asks for approval as an **inline composer card** (one pipeline for all human-in-the-loop moments); reject-with-feedback loops the agent back into planning. The mode selector keeps plan and goal mutually exclusive.

![Plan mode: the live checklist docked in the right sidebar with completed steps struck through, and the inline "Implement this plan?" approval card in the composer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/c57fe74c64e15e1de7a76e742598904ff207c849/docs/assets/interactive-parity/plan-sidebar.png)

![The exit-plan approval as an inline composer card — Approve or Revise-with-feedback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/c57fe74c64e15e1de7a76e742598904ff207c849/docs/assets/interactive-parity/plan-approval-inline.png)

### 3 · Goal mode
`/goal set "<objective>" --budget <n>` (or the chip dialog) and walk away. The driver mirrors the Codex goal extension's idle-continuation semantics, adapted honestly to OpenClaw's architecture (no idle event exists — a spike proved the safe shape first): a debounced scheduler armed **only** by turn-completion, firing **only** when four gates pass (goal active · no active run · queue empty · no-progress ceiling not hit), via the cron system-event path + a heartbeat wake. **After a fire it never self-re-arms** — cadence is structurally bounded, no tight loop. Ceiling hit → auto-pause. Budget hit → disarm. The model can only mark `complete|blocked` (host-only pause, mirroring Codex).

![The goal editor modal — objective, token budget, and Save, with the "Pursuing goal" pill live in the composer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/c57fe74c64e15e1de7a76e742598904ff207c849/docs/assets/interactive-parity/goal-editor.png)

## Security
- **Questions**: human-in-the-loop by construction — no new privilege; answers are typed user input on existing paths; resolution needs the same scopes as approval resolution; proactive push only targets the question's own turn-source chat.
- **Plan gate**: fail-closed at the single choke point, with an **in-PR adversarial suite**: exec, MCP tool, plugin tool, and subagent-spawn are each proven vetoed through the real hook.
- **Goal driver**: a driver-continued turn has exactly the privileges of a user turn — the in-PR safety test raises an exec approval *during* a driver-continued turn and it blocks normally. Layered brakes: debounce+jitter · 4 gates · durable ceiling · budget states · experimental flag (default off).

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** agents couldn't ask, couldn't plan reviewably, couldn't pursue; codex `request_user_input` degraded to plain text; `update_plan` events rendered as a bare text line.
**Evidence (full gate on the final tip, run and read by the submitting orchestrator):** 9 backend suites in one run (question manager/wire-contract integration/tool/forwarder/sweep/`/answer` · plan state machine + **adversarial bypass matrix** + approval wire-contract · goal driver loop-safety + integration probe + wiring/safety + commands + durability) — all green; `tsgo` core + test 0; UI suites 781/784 (the 3 = the long-documented `terminal-panel` fixture flake, failing identically on pristine `main` — verified); `ui:i18n:check` clean; `ui:build` 0; **full type-aware `pnpm lint` 0**. The wire-contract integration tests land IN this PR: client↔gateway param drift fails CI here, not in production.

*▶ [Full 30s narrated walkthrough (mp4)](https://github.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/releases/download/interactive-parity-media-v1/parity-demo.mp4) — questions, plan mode, the sidebar plan, inline approval, and goal mode running unattended.*

## Dependency note
No new dependencies; no lockfile change. Plan-mode semantics derive from a 156-case parity-hardened prior implementation; goal-driver semantics mirror `codex-rs/ext/goal` for cross-runtime consistency. Codex plan/goal wire bridges are documented in-code as follow-up seams (hub roadmap) — no speculative plumbing.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running an agent with `experimental.localModelLean=true` could lose the expected tool surface when overriding that agent to a non-local provider model.

In the observed failure, a fresh `main` session using `meta/muse-spark-1.1` returned `Tool exec not found`. The same fresh session worked after disabling `main.experimental.localModelLean`, which isolated the failure to local-model lean being applied outside its intended scope.

## Why This Change Was Made

`localModelLean` is intended for local coding-model runs. It was being resolved from agent/session config alone, so a non-local provider override could inherit local-model-specific tool filtering and Tool Search defaults.

This change makes local-model lean model-aware. It keeps the existing behavior for local model providers such as Ollama and llama.cpp, while preventing lean mode from applying to non-local provider overrides when runtime model context is available.

This does not change configured tool policy, session authorization, or static provider catalog metadata handling.

## User Impact

Users can keep `experimental.localModelLean=true` on local-model-oriented agents without accidentally applying that lean tool surface to cloud/provider overrides.

Local-model optimization remains available for local providers, while non-local providers keep their expected direct tool surface.

## Evidence

Before this patch:
- `main.experimental.localModelLean=true`
- fresh `main` session
- model override: `meta/muse-spark-1.1`
- result: `Tool exec not found`

Runtime isolation check:
- Setting `main.experimental.localModelLean=false` and restarting the gateway made the same fresh `main` + Meta smoke succeed.
- Exact observed output: `main-meta-fixed-tool-ok`

Focused local validation after this patch:
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --write src/agents/local-model-lean.ts src/agents/agent-tools.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts src/agents/local-model-lean.test.ts`
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/agents/local-model-lean.ts src/agents/agent-tools.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts src/agents/local-model-lean.test.ts`
- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/agents/local-model-lean.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-tool-construction-plan.test.ts`

Focused test result:
- Test Files: 2 passed
- Tests: 39 passed

Regression coverage added:
- non-local provider override does not enable lean mode
- local provider selection still enables lean mode
- non-local provider override does not inject lean Tool Search defaults

Scope note:
- This is separate from PR #103051, which is limited to static provider catalog metadata propagation.

target.title: fix: preserve prompt cache continuity in embedded sessions
target.body:
Related: #102175

## What Problem This Solves

Long-lived embedded sessions could lose prompt-cache continuity in three connected ways:

- ambient `room_event` turns changed cache-visible delivery instructions and owner-only tool schemas;
- preflight, manual, and queued compaction rebuilt prompt/tool state from the current turn's delivery mode instead of the session-stable prompt mode;
- the built-in authenticated session stream was mistaken for a custom stream, so `openai-chatgpt-responses` runs used the managed full-context SSE adapter instead of OpenClaw's native cached WebSocket continuation path.

## Fix

- Separate effective source delivery from the session-stable prompt-facing delivery mode. Room events still require `message_tool_only` delivery without rewriting the cached prompt contract. Executable message tools retain the real turn mode, while Pi and Codex use the stable mode only for model-visible prompt/tool shape.
- Keep the safe room-event owner-only core-tool inventory stable across sender changes while preserving execution authorization.
- Carry the prompt-facing mode through primary runs, queued followups, Codex app-server prompt/tool builders, and every compaction entry point; compaction now rebuilds tools and system text from that stable mode. Codex keeps reusable thread instructions stable and adds strict room-event delivery guidance only to the current turn.
- Mark OpenClaw's built-in session auth wrapper and allow only that known wrapper to select the native `openai-chatgpt-responses` stream. Unmarked custom/provider streams retain their existing routing.

The native routing check is API-based, so it covers GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 without model-version branches.

## Evidence

Redacted same-session traces from the reported Discord room-event flow showed tool inventory flipping between 44 and 47 tools and cache reads collapsing to roughly 2k-10k or ceilinging around 37k-40k. With the room-event prompt/tool fix installed, warm turns with stable inventory reached roughly 49k-52k cached tokens on approximately 51k-55k context.

The route regression test reproduces the built-in auth-wrapper misclassification. A two-turn GPT-5.6 Sol WebSocket test then proves that the native provider sends the second turn with `previous_response_id` and only the new input, rather than replaying the full context.

## Validation

Validated at head `f0d85b0829d54ec9f3bda3406168f8bf2d8c0d6d` on upstream `main` `8dedb0ebcaef2bbe6dcd7b9ad137554b62ac1d21`:

- focused regression suite: 25 project test files, 1,211 tests passed, including a real targetless room-event send through the internal source-reply sink;
- `pnpm tsgo:prod`, `pnpm check:test-types`, `pnpm tsgo:test:packages`, and the 120-plugin extension package boundary compile passed;
- changed TypeScript passed `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint`; all generated prompt snapshots are current;
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` passed.

## Boundaries

- Effective room-event delivery remains strict; this does not make private final text visible.
- Non-owner execution of owner-only tools remains blocked.
- Custom provider/session streams are not rerouted.
- Native `auto` transport may still fall back to SSE after a real WebSocket failure; this change makes the native continuation path reachable and tested, but does not claim every upstream request will be cached.

Disclaimer: This PR was filed and updated autonomously by Codex on behalf of the reporter. Private user, channel, host, credential, and full trace identifiers were removed from the evidence.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Group-channel messages need a generic way to distinguish the runtime message author from the operator/user represented by the agent session. Without source actor attribution, downstream prompts, tools, and memory adapters can only see channel/session context and may conflate another group participant with the operator. This should be solved as a channel contract, not as a deployment-specific memory backend workaround.

## Summary

- Adds a generic `SourceActor` inbound context contract for the runtime identity of the message author.
- Maps Signal sender identity into `SourceActor` without making the contract Signal-specific.
- Types `SourceActorRole` as `operator | participant | self | system | external`.
- Documents `SourceActor` as canonical and the flattened `SourceActor*` fields as scalar mirrors for prompt templates.
- Exports `SourceActorContext` and `SourceActorRole` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/reply-runtime`.

## Stack

This is stacked after #96738 and `codex/signal-mention-facts-context`. Until those land, this PR's diff will include its dependencies.

## Production impact

No behavior change by itself. The change gives prompts, tools, and memory integrations a stable way to distinguish a group participant from the operator/user. Signal direct and group senders are represented as `participant` source actors.

## Evidence

- Channel context tests cover generic `SourceActor` projection and object-to-scalar mirror parity.
- Channel contract helpers now assert `SourceActor` scalar mirrors stay in sync with the canonical structured object.
- Signal mention-gating tests cover Signal sender identity mapping into the generic context.
- Plugin SDK runtime mock tests cover `SourceActor*` parity with production inbound context.
- Focused tests passed:
  `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/channels/inbound-event/context.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/test-helpers/plugin-runtime-mock.test.ts extensions/signal/src/monitor/event-handler.mention-gating.test.ts`
- Plugin SDK API check passed without a baseline hash diff:
  `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check`
- Production TypeScript check passed:
  `pnpm tsgo:prod`

### Redacted Runtime Proof

Temporary local proof harness imported production `buildChannelInboundEventContext` and printed the emitted prompt context on PR head `5fab61f873`. target.title: fix(signal): detect native bot mentions in group gating
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Signal groups can be configured with `requireMention=true` so side chatter stays quiet until the bot is explicitly mentioned. Signal native mentions arrive as structured `dataMessage.mentions[]` metadata plus object-replacement characters in the message text. The current Signal handler renders those placeholders as `@<uuid>` or `@<phone>`, then relies on text mention regexes. Selecting the bot from Signal's native mention UI can therefore fail to wake the bot unless a matching text fallback happens to be configured.

This also leaves `canDetectMention` tied only to configured text regexes and passes `hasAnyMention=false` even when Signal supplied structured mention metadata.

## Why This Change Was Made

This patch keeps the fix inside the Signal plugin and adds a small native mention fact resolver. It compares structured Signal mention metadata against the current bot account identity:

- UUID via `channels.signal.accountUuid`
- phone number via the existing E.164 normalizer and `channels.signal.account`

The event handler now combines text fallback and native metadata:

- `wasMentioned` is true for text fallback or a native mention that targets the current bot account.
- `canDetectMention` reflects text regexes or available bot account identity.
- `hasAnyMention` reflects valid structured Signal mention metadata so the shared mention-decision contract can distinguish command bypass from messages mentioning someone else.

Mentions of other participants do not trigger the bot. Missing bot identity does not become a false mention. Existing text fallback, group access checks, pending history, attachment restraint, control-command handling, direct messages, and `requireMention=false` behavior stay unchanged.

This supersedes #69413, which was closed without merge, by adding the missing capability facts, event-handler coverage, and docs.

## User Impact

Before:

> A user could select the bot from Signal's native mention UI in a `requireMention` group and get no response because the rendered `@uuid`/`@phone` text did not match the configured agent-name regex.

After:

> Native Signal mentions targeting the current bot account pass mention gating. Mentions of other participants remain silent and are kept only as bounded pending context. A later bot mention can include recent skipped group context and reply in the same group.

Docs now describe Signal native mention behavior, `accountUuid`, text mention fallback, and a mention-gated group configuration with bounded history.

### Behavior Change

Signal groups with `requireMention=true` that have a configured bot identity (`accountUuid`/`account`) but no text mention regexes previously fell through to pass-through handling. After this change they enforce mention gating via native Signal mention metadata. Group chatter that did not mention the bot but previously reached it may now be gated. This is intended and makes native-only `requireMention` groups behave as documented. Maintainers with such groups should expect stricter, correct gating after upgrade.

### Trust Model

`dataMessage.mentions[]` is sender-supplied. A group member could craft metadata naming the bot; the only effect is waking the bot, which any member can already do via a normal Signal mention. Native facts are still validated against a real object-replacement placeholder span, so malformed metadata does not become a bot mention.

### Native Identity Note

For full native mention coverage, configure `channels.signal.accountUuid` alongside `channels.signal.account`. Phone-only identity can still match phone-backed mention metadata, but UUID-only Signal mention metadata requires `accountUuid`.

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

With groupChat.visibleReplies="automatic" and groupChat.unmentionedInbound="room_event", unmentioned group/channel messages are classified as room events and then forced to message_tool_only. That changes the generated system prompt inside the same session and reduces provider prompt-cache reuse.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start OpenClaw 2026.6.11 (e085fa1) with this redacted config shape:

```json
{

    "groupChat": {
      "visibleReplies": "automatic",
```

4. Compare generated request traces and provider prompt-cache metrics.

### Expected behavior

If visibleReplies is explicitly set to "automatic", group/channel room-event turns should preserve automatic visible final-reply semantics, or the room-event delivery mode should be separately configurable/documented. The generated system prompt should not switch between automatic final-text/NO_REPLY semantics and message_tool_only/private-final semantics inside the same session unless that switch is explicitly configured.

Observed request traces from the same session/model/cache key showed the prompt contract flipping. The session-start turn used the automatic reply prompt with `## Silent Replies`; later unmentioned room_event turns used the message-tool-only/private-final prompt. Provider cache reuse was inconsistent even with the same provider cache key.

OpenClaw 2026.6.11 (e085fa1)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (25F80)

### Install method

OpenClaw CLI/gateway via LaunchAgent, using ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json

### Model

synthetic:hf:zai-org/GLM-5.2

OpenClaw -> OpenAI-compatible proxy -> Synthetic/GLM-5.2

target.title: fix(slack): remember event-carried channel types so mpDMs key one session (#102676)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A Slack multi-party DM (`mpim`) room produces **two parallel sessions per agent**. Human-authored messages carry `channel_type: "mpim"` on the event and key `slack:group:<channelId>`; bot-authored inbound shapes omit `channel_type`, and when the `conversations.info` fill cannot resolve the type either (e.g. missing `mpim:read` scope — the fill's `catch` returns `{}`), C-prefix inference falls back to `"channel"` and keys a second `slack:channel:<channelId>` session for the same room. Modern mpDM ids are C-prefixed, so prefix inference cannot disambiguate. (`extensions/slack/src/monitor/channel-type.ts`, `message-handler/prepare.ts`; fixes #102676.)

## Why This Change Was Made

The room's type is **already known** from events previously seen for it — the fix carries that prepared fact forward instead of rediscovering (or guessing). A bounded process-local map alongside the existing channel/user caches remembers explicit `channel_type` values seen on events; the resolution chain becomes `event type → channel-info fill → remembered event type → prefix inference`. The system-event session-key resolver consults the same memory, so system events key identically (sibling surface covered).

Relative to the closed attempts on this issue: **no new network lookups** (#102752 added one and was closed for it), and it fixes the reported **C-prefixed** path mechanism itself rather than special-casing an ID prefix (#102702 only changed G-prefixed IDs). The remembered value is a *last* fallback — an explicit event type or successful `conversations.info` result always wins.

## User Impact

One session per agent per mpDM room: agents keep a single conversation context and history instead of silently splitting across `slack:group:` and `slack:channel:` keys when bots talk to each other. No config change; no new public options; no behavior change for channels whose events or info lookups already resolve a type.

## Evidence

Executed before/after (full output in the PR comment below). The regression test drives the real `prepareSlackMessage` twice on **one** monitor context (real `createSlackMonitorContext`), with `resolveChannelName` returning `{}` — a human `mpim` message for `C0MPDM42`, then a same-room message **without** `channel_type`:

```
BEFORE — main's context.ts/prepare.ts + this test:
  × keeps one mpDM classification when a later event omits channel_type (#102676)
    Error: Expected Slack message to be prepared
  Tests  1 failed | 113 passed (114)
  (the typeless same-room message stops being an mpDM: dropped under default room
   mention-gating, or keyed as the parallel slack:channel:C0MPDM42 session)

AFTER — this PR:
  Tests  114 passed (114)
  human msg    → ChatType "group", From "slack:group:C0MPDM42"
  typeless msg → ChatType "group", From "slack:group:C0MPDM42"   (one classification)
```

Sibling context suites (`inbound-context.contract`, `prepare-thread-context`, `prepare.thread-session-key`) 32/32 green; `pnpm tsgo:extensions` **0 errors**; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean. Commands: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.test.ts` (and sibling files); before-run used `git checkout upstream/main -- extensions/slack/src/monitor/context.ts extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.ts`.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
